utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, on November 15th on three occasions you testified that you were not aware of the mistreatment of prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as we mentioned yesterday, Bosanski Samac was -- is not a very large metropolis, like New York or Tokyo. It's a small area.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, everything is relative. For somebody it can be a small town. For somebody it can be quite large.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, compared to New York City, Tokyo, Chicago --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. We've been through all these topics yesterday. I don't see any reason why we are repeating this story. Let's go directly with the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Do avoid repetition. It implies that you're finished with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Far from it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you recalled witnesses have testified of beatings during outside of the police station. You've heard witnesses testify in this trial beatings occurred outside of the police station, in the street area in front of the police station.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard -- the war was going on. The shells were landing everywhere, and the residents didn't move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm saying beatings. You recall there was testimony by Muhamed Bicic, Hasan Bicic, that beatings occurred in front of the SUP or police station. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking if you saw it. Do you recall the testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the testimony about the beatings that occurred in the courtyard -- outside in the courtyard at the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the testimony that when prisoners arrived in May, there was shooting and beatings outside of the high school area? Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall testimony from witnesses that they had to sing Chetnik songs very loudly, sometimes for hours at a time, and this was at the school and at the Territorial Defence building? Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall testimony of witnesses, at least two witnesses, that they would hear screams and cries all night long from the police station, from the Territorial Defence building, and from the schools? Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, do you recall the testimony about prisoners being brought to the local hospital or prisoners on occasional -- occasionally being visited by doctors or nurses at the various detention facilities? Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, over an eight-month period, basically from April to the end of the year, no one other than Stevan Todorovic -- no, I'm sorry, not even Stevan Todorovic -- no one ever spoke to you about the beatings, no one? Or what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For the most part of that period, I was not in Samac. And I've said this many times so far. Secondly, Stevan Todorovic never reported on any kind of mistreatment of prisoners, nor did he ever submit any kind of written report to the Municipal Assembly of Samac to that effect nor did he speak to me about that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Fine. We know about Stevan Todorovic. He never mentioned it. But did any resident -- my question to you is going to be: Did any resident in that eight-month period ever approach you about the beating of their friends or relatives? Did any resident ever approach you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We are here trying to find a needle in a stack of hay. The war was going on. Shells were landing everywhere. There were burials every day. Many wounded, lack of money, poverty, no electricity, no water supply, wounded people, prosthesis, quadriplegics, paraplegics, haemodialysis, vaccinations, you name it. There wasn't a single problem that the municipality was not faced with, and every single resident of that municipality. When I went to work, I had so many problems that it was hard to deal with that and to survive in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that that's a special kind of art.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, just what I'm talking about. You were hearing about all of these problems from fellow Crisis Staff members, from fellow municipal officials, from residents. Did one of these persons from the Crisis Staff, from the executive council, from any municipal employee or official, any resident of Samac ever tell you that people were being beaten in the detention facilities; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned as part of your humanitarian obligation you would try and assist and help out at the hospitals. Did any doctor, nurse, or hospital employee tell you that we have beaten prisoners coming in, or we're going out to the hospitals and there are terribly beaten prisoners? Did that happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I've told you that I was mostly involved in haemodialysis, that I tried to assist in treatment of chronic patients, and that we gave last penny in order to keep people of all ethnicities alive. In addition to that, I put in extra effort in order to try to obtain vaccinations. I tried to provide medicine and vaccinations to residents of all ethnicities. In addition to that, I attended some 500 funerals. We had 583 killed, people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, the question was straightforward did anybody tell you that there had been prisoners who had been badly beaten, from the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one short question. Dr. Simic, did you ever during the period from April 17th, 1992 and the following months, did you ever enter the TO, the SUP, the elementary, or the high school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one other question: Did you ever walk past those buildings, all of them or any one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible, but not very -- on very few occasions, because that was the war zone. My offices were several kilometres away from that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you find out about all these beatings?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In the later period of time, when we -- as we tried to remove Stevan Todorovic from office, his shortcomings and work at the Ministry of the Interior emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you indicated that you weren't aware of isolation. Were you aware of any mass arrests in Bosanski Samac of the non-Serb population? And when I say "mass," I mean large numbers, hundreds.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I had the information on Crkvina and that Stevan Todorovic informed me that people had been returned to their homes on the same day with apologies. I was informed about Zasavica, but that was not prison at any time. Secondly, I told you that Stevan Todorovic had informed the War Presidency that he had some prisoners against whom he was gathering documents and that he was about to file criminal complaints, that he had enough material to file criminal complaints and to put those people to trial. And how can a civilian organ interfere in the work of the military and the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, maybe I'm wrong, but I heard something which is not consistent with the transcript. Actually, it relates to page 6, line 8, the sentence beginning, "I was informed about Zasavica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not so sure that that was the words of Dr. Simic. Maybe my colleague can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as I told you yesterday, you've already mentioned the Stevan Todorovic matter. I'm not talking about what you heard from Stevan Todorovic and I'm not talking about Crkvina. My question to you is: Do you agree that you've stated you were never advised of any mass arrests? Is that what your testimony is? You were never aware or advised of any mass arrests of the non-Serb population in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I've just answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, sir. As I said to you, other than what you've heard from Stevan Todorovic and other than what you've mentioned from Crkvina, you were never aware of any mass arrests in Bosanski Samac; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that answer. The interpreters couldn't --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any other arrests? You said during your case -- you spoke of Zasavica and prison in Samac and Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So I take it -- sir, so I take it that you're stating that you weren't aware of any other arrests other than what you heard from Stevan Todorovic and Crkvina, the Crkvina incident. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Except for those about which Stevan Todorovic informed the Crisis Staff and War Presidency. He did not inform me personally. Nobody was in charge of informing me personally on any matter. I was a member of a joint body, not civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you heard -- you heard me read the testimony from Exhibit 141 at page 43 where Simo Zaric said that "People were detained in the two schools. It was all well known." Do you recall me reading that? Do you recall me reading that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: You didn't read it out in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read from page 43, Simo Zaric's interview, Exhibit 141. "How was it then that you know that the Crisis Staff is the one who made the decision to isolate these people in Zasavica?" "It was no secret. It was a well-known fact. Everything that was decided was well known. For instance, that people were going to be taken to Crkvina and that they were going to be detained in the two schools, it was all well known. There was no secret about it." Do you recall me reading that to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I've already said to you that in Crkvina and in schools there were no prisoners at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall me reading that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Weiner. And maybe you can get back to -- I don't know if it will interrupt your flow, but I don't think you've dealt with the clarification that Mr. Pantelic raised, which was page 6, lines 8 and 9, where Dr. Simic said, in the English, "I was informed about Zasavica, but that was not prison at any time." And Mr. Pantelic had said that he wasn't sure whether the transcript reflected -- it was -- reflected actually what Dr. Simic had said. But don't let me interrupt your flow. Maybe you can, though, come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let me ask that question. Is that what you had just said, that Zasavica was not a prison? Was that your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a prison. It wasn't a prison ever, nor was it possible to turn such a large territory into a prison, nor can two policemen guard such a vast territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But the problem is with the first part of that sentence. I was informed or yesterday I informed you. So it's -- there is some misunderstanding with that regard. So could you clarify that with the defendant, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll clarify that next as something that was said before the screen goes away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just also want to clarify your statement, "I've already said to you that in Crkvina and in the schools, there were no prisoners at any time." Are you now saying there were never any prisoners in the schools? You just said that. It's on line 13, page 8.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't say in that way. I said that in Crkvina schools, there were no prisoners ever, that in schools in Crkvina there were no prisoners ever. Crkvina has schools too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- that's the way I understood the defendant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The other question, sir, is from -- Mr. Pantelic wanted something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think it's quite simple, Mr. Weiner. It's the words "I was informed about Zasavica." That's what's in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question "I was informed about Zasavica." When were you informed about Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war we started a farm operation there. The owners of the farms were mostly Croats. We had a fair relation with that. They started farm production. We took the food they produced over from them. Can I explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. The question is: When were you informed about Zasavica and the happenings at Zasavica? When?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When I came back from my sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So at the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right, sir. I just read to you the statement from Simo Zaric that it was public knowledge about prisoners being detained at the two schools in Bosanski Samac. I'd like to read to you a statement from the joint motion for consideration of plea agreement between Milan Simic and the Office of the Prosecutor, paragraph C, 8C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. We as Defence never saw this agreement, specifically this part of C, 8C. I never discussed this motion or content of this motion with my client. He is not absolutely ready to respond on any issue with regard to this plea bargain agreement because the Defence was not provided with the adequate materials. End of story. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a public document. This is not a private document. It's a public document that Milan Simic pled. The hearings were open. All I'm saying to him is Zaric knew about it, Milan Simic knew about it, I'm going to tell him that Miroslav Tadic knew about it, and you as the Crisis Staff and War Presidency president didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, we are wondering -- because the plea agreement remained confidential and there was an order clarifying which part of the proceedings were to be in the -- in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was under the impression that the confidentiality was lifted off the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: With everything else except the plea agreement, if you read the judgment, you'll find it in there. And there was an order actually clarifying what was to be in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So this part of the plea agreement which still remains confidential cannot be put to the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, Mr. Tadic has testified -- I'm sorry, has provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. On 26 March, 1998 at pages 28 and 29 of Exhibit 138:

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Tadic, you know that dozens if not hundreds of men were arrested in that week after the takeover, or detained at the police station and at camps in Samac. Some of these were old men, as you like to describe yourself, much older than you. At least one of these men was a Catholic priest. Why were all these people being arrested? You mean to tell me every single one of these men was arrested because they were concealing weapons?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I was talking about the first days of the war. I was talking about those days. I was talking about the 18th, 19th, the 20th, those first days of the war. I think that not more than 30 were arrested then and there's no question that a large number of people were arrested then -- there's no question that a large number of people were arrested then. What you're talk about, the mass arrests that took place, I think possibly a month later. Sir, you've heard that, do you know any reason why Mr. Tadic would say that if it wasn't true, that mass arrests took place a month later? We're talking about May of 1992. Do you know any reason why he would say that if it wasn't true, sir?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I would rather you asked me about my opinion. I cannot comment on somebody else's opinion. That's his opinion. And authorities is a very complex term. When you say "authorities," one needs to define exactly which authority one has in mind. I knew four types of authorities. I wish to testify myself, not give comments on somebody else' testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Do you know why Mr. Tadic, not offering an opinion, would state a fact that mass arrests took place sometime in May if it wouldn't true? Do you know any reason; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on to another topic. You testified that you took certain -- that the Crisis Staff took certain actions based on orders and decisions coming down from the republic level. Do you recall that testimony last week?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you testified that the republic enactments superseded municipal ones. You testified to that on November 14th, at page 90. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was always that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. You also testified that you were duty-bound to respect the Serb Autonomous District, the SAO decisions. You testified to that also on November 14th. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We accepted or wished to observe the decisions of the SAO, but I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified that you were duty-bound to respect those; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I testified that we respected the laws of Republika Srpska, but I also testified that we wished to join the SAO Semberija and Majevica. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You can explain on redirect, sir -- actually, all I'm asking you is if you testified that you respected the decisions. I'm not interested in when you wanted to join, why you wanted to join that SAO. My question is: Did you respect the decisions that came out of that -- that or any SAO that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Now, that is a legal question. I don't know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did you testify on page 90 of November 14th that you were duty-bound to respect the Serb Autonomous District decisions? Did you testify to that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to respect everything that was in accordance with the law, and the SAO is a constitutional category.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you this document, sir. Sir, are you familiar with that document, or do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's dated April 26, 1992, and it concerns the instructions for the operation of Crisis Staff headquarters of Serb people in the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The 26th of April, yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's the instructions for the operation of crisis headquarters of Serb people in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could we look at paragraph 3. It says: "Crisis headquarters coordinates government functions for the purpose of protecting the territory, safety of the population and its properties, setting up authority and organisation of all other forms of life and work." When it says "safety of the population and its properties," it does not state only the Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "no," you're saying no, it does not state only the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That does not pertain to the Serb population only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we move on to paragraph 6, it says: "The operation of the crisis headquarters is based on constitutional and legal provisions and also on the decisions of the assembly, presidency, and the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's just as you had previously said. You have to follow the decisions that come down from above, as you've previously testified; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: But item 3 itself says that the Crisis Staff is the coordinator. It coordinates. It does not carry out. It coordinates. It makes it possible for the state authorities to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're on item 6, and it says: "The operation of the crisis headquarters is based on constitutional and legal provisions and also on the decisions of the assembly, presidency, and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." As you've testified, you have to follow the laws that come down from above; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. We were not the executive government. We did not execute. The executive government is a special type of government. We coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Even in coordination, you have to follow the laws and the rules that come down above from the assembly. You have to abide by the laws of the constitution, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: But we do not implement this and execute it. It is the executive that executes and implements this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Even in coordination you have to follow the laws and the rules that come down from the assembly. You have to abide by the laws of the constitution, don't you? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's the way it is in any state. The laws of that state are observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 10 states: "Towards non-combat population and the wounded, behave in an utterly humane manner and in compliance with the International Red Cross. Treat the prisoners of war in a humane manner and according to the laws of the Serb Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, we've talked about -- and you've just mentioned that Mr. Todorovic told you that prisoners were being held. And you also recall that you've testified on November 15th, when he told you prisoners were being held, he wasn't even making any sense about it, and you said that's because he was a substance abuser. Knowing that Mr. Todorovic was arresting people, what steps did you take in accordance with number 10, your rule number 10, to ensure that the prisoners were being treated humanely? What steps did the Crisis Staff take in accordance with number 10 of these instructions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That is the question that you put to me that I like the most. The Crisis Staff was coordinator; that is to say, it was not carrying out or implementing decisions but coordinating. We all came to the conclusion that the Ministry of the Interior in Samac was performing poorly. We did not want any prisoners in Samac. We reacted. And since Stevan Todorovic was appointed by the Ministry of the Interior, he was on their payroll, they were his bosses, we tried, by way of coordination, to achieve that the Ministry of the Interior in Samac carries out its job properly, without any prisoners involved. We talked to high officials of the Ministry of the Interior. One of them recommended -- his name is Tomo Kovac. He recommended to Stevan Todorovic that he resign and that he withdraw on his own. He didn't want to do it but he talked about the episode himself. Then we called the chief of Stevan Todorovic, Andrija Bilosevic to Samac to the offices of the War Presidency, and with a major apology because we were discussing the work of the Ministry of the Interior, this decree prohibits this, that we should be involved in the matters related to the military and the police. We presented our opinion that the Ministry of the Interior in Samac was not carrying out its duties, that Stevan Todorovic is not worthy of that job. And we asked Andrija Bilosevic to exercise some more control over his own service in Samac. Andrija Bilosevic was very angry of us and he left the offices of the War Presidency demonstratively. But he did turn to his branch of the Ministry of the Interior in Samac. After a few days he took all prisoners from Samac and he took them to Batkovic, over 100 kilometres away from Samac. And that is where they were under the control of the military. And it was made possible for them to be tried by a military court. Furthermore, he established a commission, because the Ministry of the Interior has inspectors, its own inspectors, and he established a commission of inspectors that came to Samac to check the work of Stevan Todorovic and the Ministry of the Interior. That commission stayed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Speak slowly. The interpreter is almost running. Can you just speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that all happened at the end of --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do apologise for hurrying this much. I get carried away by my emotions a bit, so I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: But please let me -- please let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...at the end of the year, what did you do in April, in May, and in June? What actions did you take? What orders did you issue? What letters did you send out in April, May, and June? Even July, before you shot yourself in the leg, what actions did you take in those four months in compliance with objective number 10? What orders did you issue? What letters were written?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Again, it should be known that we were cut off from the outside world, that we were in total encirclement, that we had only five telephones, five telephone lines, that these five telephone lines were under the absolute control of Stevan Todorovic, because his girlfriend worked at the phone exchange, and I could not have a single telephone conversation without Stevan Todorovic eavesdropping on me -- or rather, his girlfriend eavesdropping on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did you issue any orders or write any letters in April, May, June, or July about the safety of the prisoners? Did you issue any orders in that time, April, May, June, or July?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Give me a description from the instructions. It was prohibited to us -- we were prohibited from interfering in the military and police. But we tried as human beings to exercise some influence so that the Ministry of the Interior in war conditions in the very unfavourable conditions of a civil war, because we are now shedding light on one segment only and there are many, many segments there --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, again my question is: Did you issue any orders or write any letters in April, May, June, or July about the safety of the prisoners? Did you issue any orders? And meaning "you," did the Crisis Staff in April, May, June, or July? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In writing? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The final paragraph is 13. And once again, these are instructions for the Crisis Staff. "War profiteers, pillage groups may -- and so on have to be arrested and hand over to the investigation court of the Republika Srpska." Did the Crisis Staff issue any order in April, May, June, July requesting the investigation or the prosecution of looters, any written orders or any written decisions? Did the Crisis Staff issue any?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff put forth a request to the Ministry of the Interior to have judges demobilised. The Crisis Staff appointed a coordinator for creating conditions and for establishing civilian courts, and we also helped military courts so that the military authority could function properly. So that has to do with the military judiciary. We managed to demobilise four judges and we established a court, and there are decisions of the People's Assembly establishing a civilian court in Samac and a prosecutor's office in Samac and three judges from Samac went to Bijeljina, that is to say, that we created conditions for the functioning of the state so that every branch of government would do its own job, so that the judiciary would do their job, the executive their job, and the legislative their job. Unfortunately there was this fourth authority, and that was the military authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question again is: Did the Crisis Staff issue any written orders -- I'll add the word "written orders" -- in April, May, June, or July requiring the investigation of prosecution of looters -- actually, I'll read the question. Did the Crisis Staff issue any order in April, May, June, or July, requiring the investigation or the prosecution of looters? Any written orders, any written decisions, did the Crisis Staff issue any? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That is the job of judges in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We ensured the work of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the judiciary wasn't doing their job, so my question is again: Did the Crisis Staff issue any order in April, May, June, July requesting the investigation or the prosecution of looters, any written orders or any written decision, did the Crisis Staff issue any? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I have answered you already in terms of how we worked. By encouraging and creating conditions for the functioning of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once again, that's not the question -- the question is: Did -- I'll read it again. Did the Crisis Staff issue any order in April, May, June, July requesting the investigation or the prosecution of looters? Any written orders or any written decisions, did the Crisis Staff issue any? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It issued a request to the Ministry of Defence to demobilise judges, to establish courts, and for them to do their job. We thought that it was only in that way, by strengthening the state itself and by strengthening the system, that we can prevent looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's a written decision that was issued?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a written request to the Ministry of Defence to demobilise judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what date was that issued?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was during the first days of the war. There are decisions of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska when the court of law in Samac is being established, when the prosecutor's office in Samac is being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking you is: In response to the looting, because you've admitted in May and June -- not first days of the war -- you saw looted -- you called them plundered vehicles. What action did you take? What written decisions or written orders were taken by the Crisis Staff in response to those -- that looting and plundering? Were there any written decisions or written orders? So if you first saw it in May and June, we're talking about May and June. Not at the beginning when you're saying, "Let's get the courts going. Let's get things happening." What written decisions? Did you call for investigations? Did the Crisis Staff issue an order calling for investigations of looting and plundering? Are there written decisions; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I have answered that question for you three times already. We thought that by strengthening the state, by strengthening the judiciary, that that is the only way in which we can stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the Crisis Staff did not issue any written decisions because the Crisis Staff authorised the looting by paramilitaries and the military and by private citizens, the Crisis Staff authorised it. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did not allow any looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to read to you an excerpt from Simo Zaric's statement, Exhibit 141, his statement from pages 51/52. It's his statement of April 2nd, 1998. It's a long excerpt, but he's talking about get away from the Odzak part of it. "The part of Odzak municipality was attached to the Samac municipality." And he's referring to something in Odzak. Then he gets on:

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I can tell you in two sentences what happened to the property. Let us say that perhaps one section was used for the needs of the Army of Republika Srpska. Of course, soldiers had to live and eat -- I'm sorry, eat and live. Everything else had been looted and taken into private ownership by others, put into the pockets of others. The factors of criminalisation was very evident. Not only among young people, but also among the troops, the army. From the very beginning of the war, this was tolerated, which is why anarchy ruled, which is why criminals had power in their hands. They were allowed to do whatever they wanted. They never had a better opportunity for looting than then. And they would never have done it had not their leadership had allowed them to do so."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So this was the Samac Crisis Staff who was allowing this looting to go on?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many things were taken away. It was all organised by them. Many things were also hidden from me and I don't known where things were taken, but I know that many things were taken away -- I'm sorry, were taken then. And since then, the municipality of Vukosavljevica, has been formed there. Now Serbs live and the SDS ruled [Realtime transcript read in error "suicide SDS"] and there had been a strong polarisation between them now, precisely because of all this property that the Crisis Staff have smuggled away somewhere. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic personally benefitted from any of this looting?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot be sure, but compared to me they have a much better lifestyle. They could not possibly have made that kind of money during this war. Sir, are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would accuse you of thievery and being -- you and the Crisis Staff being involved in the looting if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. There is some misunderstanding here in the transcript. Page 24 -- page 24, line 1. The sentence, "Now Serbs live and the suicide SDS." Is that the accurate version that you -- although we could always discuss about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. "Now Serbs lived and the SDS ruled," should be the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, my question is: Sir, are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would accuse you of thievery, you and the Crisis Staff of thievery, you and the Crisis Staff of being involved in the looting if it wasn't true? Do you know of any reason?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question. I absolutely disagree with that statement from the first to the last word and I will prove that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know of any bias or prejudice on Mr. Zaric's part which would make him give a false statement against you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to comment upon his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then let us move on to another piece of legislation. Sir, we talked about you being one of the delegates or a representative to the National Assembly of the Serbian People. We -- there are different words for "representative." My question is -- to you is: Did you attend May 12th, 1992 session of the National Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you attend that session?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware as the president of the Crisis Staff as well as the representative -- one of the representatives to that delegation or that body, that at that meeting both Karadzic and Krajisnik called for the separation of the Serb population from the two other ethnic communities? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That is a hypothetical question. I do not believe in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You do not believe in that? Let me quote Mr. Karadzic, talking about the goals. Okay. Let me read --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would be very grateful if my learned friend can give us certain information where we can find this exhibit or this document; otherwise, it's a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Difficult for you to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Complicated for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just going to read a few sentences. But if you -- I can avoid that. We can go right to Exhibit 5, where there is the decision where they list those six goals, those six strategic objectives or goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of Krajisnik and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's use the exhibit then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that decision in front of you is signed by the president -- or it's from the president of the National Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik; correct? Is that who it's from?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The signature is that of Momcilo Krajisnik, and this comes from the National Assembly. This decision of Momcilo Krajisnik, this is a decision of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Because this kept changing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, strategic objective number 1: "Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you please read strategic objective number 1.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: "State delineation from other two ethnic communities."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, how did the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac or the Municipality of Bosanski Samac implement strategic objective number 1?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: You're saying that as though that was a law. It was no law at all. It was not a decree. It was an objective. We changed from day to day. Prior to that the Lisbon Agreement had been signed. The Lisbon Agreement was signed by the Serb side, just like the Dayton Accords were. So the objectives changed. Objectives were not law, and they were not mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, what is the date of that strategic objectives? What's the date of that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we could clarify also when it was published too, if there is certain date on the headings of the Official Gazette, just for the sake of clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It says, "Official Gazette of the Serbian People in BH, number 3/92."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is -- I asked you how it was published, and you said things changed, and you said the Lisbon Agreement had been signed. But you are aware, sir, that on the 24th -- between the 24th and the 26th, both the HDZ and the SDA had renounced the Lisbon Agreement and it ended.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Lisbon Agreement, or rather, Cutilheiro Plan, the plan of the European Union, Mr. Cutilheiro worked until the summer of 1992 on its implementation, and I think that he's disappointed to this day that it hasn't been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you -- well, sir, you would also know that Cutilheiro on May 11th, 1992 cancelled any further meetings on cantonisation. So there were no further meetings on cantonisation or the Lisbon Plan. There was a constitutional meeting on the constitutional basis in June or July, but there was never any further meetings. So my question back to you is: Since the Lisbon Plan was over and Cutilheiro had cancelled the further cantonisation plans, how did you implement strategic objective number 1, "Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities"?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is no law at all, and nobody had a duty to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, was not the transferring of large numbers of non-Serbs out of Samac by means of the exchange programme in accordance with objective number 1 of the strategic objectives of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Doesn't that fall right in accordance with that objective?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In Samac municipality, only 3 per cent of residents were exchanged. Only 3 per cent of the population. And that was done pursuant to five agreements signed by three warring parties under the auspices of the ICRC in Budapest and in Geneva on the 22nd of May, 1992. Five agreements were signed by three warring parties regarding the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the people who were exchanged out of Bosanski Samac were non-Serbs. Isn't the exchange of non-Serbs in accordance with objective number 1, "Establish state borders separating Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities"? The non-Serbs were leaving and Serbs were coming in. You were establishing almost an ethnically pure Serbian community. Isn't that in accordance with strategic objective number 1?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: By way of exchange, people left but also came. Muslims and Croats and people of other ethnicity came as well. We are now forgetting all other nations, such as Yugoslavs, Macedonians, Montenegrins, Romas, Jews, and so on. We are forgetting all other nations that lived there then and that still live there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you again is: In Bosanski Samac, by exchanging the Muslims and Croats for Serbs, were you not acting in accordance with the strategic objectives of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, objective number 1? You were separating the Serbs from the non-Serbs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One last area I'd like to talk to you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 99, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I show you Exhibit P99. It was sent to Belgrade. Whom was is that letter sent to?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: To the Federal Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it says "the president."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was the president?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: A Croat, Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the letter describes the plight of the Serb civilians of Odzak; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The witnesses who wrote these letters can tell you more about this. I only signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it indicates that the civilians were subjected to physical terror, maltreatment, starvation, forced labour, and other brutal means -- I'm sorry, and other methods of brutal abuse, including execution. And it also notes that some prisoners were moved outside of Bosnia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here, that some detained Serbs had been transferred across the Sava River to Croatia into concentration camps, and we have not been able to establish their number yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this case, here, there has been the evidence of the same conduct. Specifically we've heard from witnesses -- the testimony of witnesses, plus one defendant who's pled guilty and has admitted to, in addition to the witnesses who have described, beatings, torture, executions or murder, forced labour, starvation, sexual assault, and prisoners being moved outside of Bosnia. We've heard testimony of that in this case too, haven't we, sir? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what your witness stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, what you have described as an inhumane situation in Odzak also has happened in -- to the non-Serb population of Samac; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Not nearly that way, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you state that answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Nothing even remotely similar happened to them in Samac, similar to what happened to Serbs in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your letter you talk about physical terror. Hasn't there been testimony here about physical terror by some witnesses?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you saw it. Was there testimony in this case of physical terror, beatings and torture? Was there testimony of that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there testimony of maltreatment?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there testimony of starvation, of being -- getting little food?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But nobody said that I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm just asking if there was testimony. Was there testimony here of people having to perform forced labour? You've heard that testimony.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You've heard testimony of other methods of abuse. You've heard the statements of Stevan Todorovic and the terrible things he had done.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But those were all your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you've heard testimony of executions, Crkvina 16 people murdered.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But those were your witnesses again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've also heard testimony from various prisoners that they were moved by helicopter to Serbia, outside of Bosnia. You've heard that testimony too. From Izet Izetbegovic, who you've stated that you're very fond of, you've heard that testimony too; correct? So those same factors which you use in your letter to describe an inhumane situation, there's testimony that that all happened here. So such -- there's testimony that that also existed in Bosanski Samac to the non-Serb population; correct? Those same factors, according to testimony, also existed in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what the testimony has been so far in this case, that that same situation, an inhumane situation, based on the factors which you've stated, there's been testimony in this case that that same inhumane situation occurred to the non-Serb civilians of Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Can I describe the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All I'm saying is the factors that you've listed, those eight factors to establish an inhumane system, there's been testimony to all of those here in this case, indicating an inhumane system in Samac existed; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't the only letter you've written. Didn't you also on May 15th write a letter to Radovan Karadzic, among other things, asking for his assistance in gaining the release of the Serbs of Odzak? Didn't you also send a letter to Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Can I see that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have a number, exhibit number. Is that -- Your Honour, do we have that in our specification?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's not in evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So then I don't see how we can discuss that, because it's even new for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's asked for -- I'm just asking if he wrote a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm his lawyer, my friend. So I'm not going into the discussion of the document that the Defence never saw and was never in a situation to discuss with the client. Simply as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You'll be able to deal with it in re-examination. The witness has challenged the Prosecution to produce the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had no -- I had no -- I just was going to ask him if he'd written the letter. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My duty as a Defence counsel is to prevent that, even if he's trying to see this document. Just as a matter of rules, Your Honour, I don't go -- I'm sure that my client will explain what is -- there is nothing, I believe, contentious, I would say. But it's simply a rule. That's my duty as a Defence counsel, to prevent my client to discuss a matter with the Prosecution prior to discuss this same matter with the Defence. And I am -- we were not in that situation, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But that's an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did he write the letter? I'm not trying to introduce the letter. I have no intention of introducing the letter. Did he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just go ahead. Let him look at the letter. And proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you write a letter to Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does it refresh your recollection if you -- if I told you that you wrote a letter on May 15th telling him about the terrible situation in Odzak and asking him and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to intervene? Do you recall signing and sending a letter out to Radovan Karadzic about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's not impossible, but I don't remember that letter and I would like to be given an opportunity to see it. We sent letters to people every three or four days. That was the only thing we could do in order to try and obtain assistance. We sent letters to all the addresses that we had, where we thought that people could help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever send out any letters to Karadzic or Krajisnik requesting an investigation for the release of the non-Serb civilians being held in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I've answered that question already three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, could you do it a fourth time did you ever send a letter to Krajisnik or Karadzic requesting an investigation into the prisoners -- the non-Serb civilians being held in Samac or requesting that they take some action or intervention to release those non-Serb civilians being held in Samac? Did you ever send a letter to Krajisnik or Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We did everything we could in order to re-establish the judiciary and have the judiciary do its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you send a letter -- we have Exhibit 99 here, which is a letter you sent to the Federal executive council in Belgrade. Did you send a letter on behalf of the non-Serb civilians, the residents of your municipality, that were being held in Samac. Did you send that letter to the federal executive council, to Krajisnik, to Karadzic? Did you send a letter to any of those three persons or groups?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm saying to you in which ways we tried to solve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Did you send a letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, that has belaboured -- you won't get the answer you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think it's obvious, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just go back to one more matter on your letter, sir. You indicate here in your letter, Exhibit 99, "We have proposed --" okay. "The Crisis Staff of our municipality has constantly been trying to reach an agreement on the resolution of the issue of the detained Serbs and in that respect we have proposed that they be exchanged." Who were you planning to exchange these Serbs of Odzak with, the 4.000 Serbs being held in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Who were you planning to exchange these people for?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We proposed to the republic commission to participate in the exchange process, and the exchange was defined by an agreement signed between the three warring parties in Geneva and in Budapest under the auspices of the ICRC. There are five agreements altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, who were you going to exchange the Serbs of Odzak for? Who?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That agreement has a stipulation where it says that there must be a consensus reached between all three warring sides when the exchange is being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, who were you going to exchange the Serbs of Odzak for? Who? The prisoners? The civilians? Who were you going to exchange them for?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That was within the scope of authorities of the exchange commission, within the Ministry of Justice, on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who were you going to exchange them for, sir? Not who was going to implement it. Not who was going to make decisions. Who? You were going to exchange them, sir, for the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We wanted them to be released without any exchange at all, because all these people wanted was to leave. The ICRC took them, trying to have them leave the Odzak municipality. The ICRC was at the head of that column which was later stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your letter says that we propose that they be exchanged. Were you not going to exchange the 4.000 Serbs of Odzak for the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac? Who were you going to exchange them for, sir? The non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: You're putting a question to me and answering it at the same time. I told you that that was a task of the exchange commission. There were several proposals in the letter, and one of them was the one you mentioned. But that's what -- in the letter. When you are trying to save people's lives, to save the population, to find a solution in wartime, that doesn't have to be malevolent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Helping people does not have to be motivated by bad will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were trying to help the non-Serb -- the Serb population of Odzak. Who were you going to exchange them for? You said that you were proposing an exchange. Who were you going to exchange them for? The only ones you could would be the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct? You can say yes. You can say no. Who were you going to exchange them for if it wasn't the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's not correct, because the exchange was conducted on all three sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a very complex issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: And other co-accused will testify to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the fact that you did not write any letters to the Federal government or to Krajisnik and Karadzic for the release of the non-Serb population or to investigate the detention of the non-Serb population, since you needed those people to be exchanged. You wanted those people held. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated at first that you were cut off from the rest of the world. Then a few minutes later in your testimony you indicated that you were sending three to four letters out a week. You didn't send one of those three to four letters out a week about the release of the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember all of the letters that were written at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you don't recall any letters written on behalf of the non-Serb population, the release of the non-Serb population being detained in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember all of the letters that I wrote at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, if you --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any bad intentions with respect to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you exchanged the non-Serb population of Samac for the Serb population of Odzak, you would be acting in accordance with objective 1, that we just described in Exhibit 5. You would separate the Serbs from the non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, and that was not a directive at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then who were you going to exchange for the Serbs of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: You should put that question to the exchange commissions on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, the exchange commissions didn't write that letter. You wrote that letter. And since you won't answer the question and you refuse to answer it, I'll finish with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out, Mr. Weiner, about the document which was discussed, which was an excerpt from the instructions for the operation of crisis headquarters, the one you discussed with the accused, by president of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could I move that as an exhibit, since he's indicated that he was familiar with the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we didn't find out when Dr. Simic became familiar with this document. Maybe during this trial or before. And secondly, Your Honour, under the P128, I believe, we already have one document with -- which is ID -- with the -- well, it's hard to know. It's an absolutely new document that we've got this morning. My recollection is that the letter font is absolutely different that we have previously, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't know what is inside. We haven't discussed that with the -- I haven't discussed that with my client, this new document. And there are many, many issues. The basic one is if -- if allegedly that's the same document that we already have in our exhibit list, so why we should make a double -- a double admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that being on our exhibit list. If he's aware of that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Because I was wondering whether we have it. It doesn't seem to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during the break we could take a look at this. But I think that this document under this heading and under this date was introduced as an ID document P128 and D31/2. It was an ID document as well. When there was talk about Variant A and B, I think that Ms. Catharine Baen spoke of it. So I think that it was introduced twice but as an identification document only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, if I may interrupt you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a similar document -- it's a similar document. It's not the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In which -- to what extent it's similar? With the content of the document or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Content is similar, but it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, simply, Your Honour, if that is the case, then we are in problem. The Defence was just aware this morning of that document. So we cannot give any -- any comment on that. If there is not -- if this document is not the same with the previous -- previously admitted document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, can you take note of this document and find out whether we haven't got it and clear this matter. We can deal with it later. And then Defence can also look at it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And another matter, Your Honour, if you'll allow me: Since we've been provided with the one binder of documents at the closing hours on Tuesday, I believe, I was never in a situation to discuss the content of this binder with my client. And I -- I informed this Trial Chamber prior to cross-examination of Dr. Simic, and you told me that after the cross-examination we could discuss that matter. I need at least one hour to go through all these documents, since many of them are not translated, so I have personally to inform my client about the content of these documents and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then we'll resume our proceedings at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We shall resume our proceedings at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Simic, during the cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked you a few questions about document 5 -- P [As interpreted]. I would like you to look at Article 2 now, Article 2 of this decision. And please answer my question. In practice, did you advocate your personal interest in the organs of the SAO Semberija and Majevica, you as an individual?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you duty-bound to respect the decisions of that institution, or rather, the Crisis Staff, the Municipal Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac, which were instructions for your own action in the organs of the SAO Semberija and Majevica?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a few examples what this looked like. Actually, please explain this to the Trial Chamber. In some decisions or instructions -- I mean, were they discussed at the Crisis Staff? How were decisions reached? And how shall I put this? These instructions for the protection of the interests of the local municipality of Samac, how were they formulated and what were the instructions you had from them? Of course, if you remember. Just in a few words can you explain this mechanism to us.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: These decisions were reached during the war, that is to say, the 21st of May, 1992. In conditions of war, this was a question of life, not mere window dressing. Samac was over 150 kilometres away from the centre of the SAO Semberija and Majevica, which was in the town of Ugljevik [phoen]. In this document we expressed our wish to become part of this SAO, primarily so that we could take part in the distribution of oil, humanitarian aid, and all the other resources that were being distributed among the municipalities. So the main objective was - and we ourselves wanted this - we were trying to get into the distribution of oil, humanitarian aid, et cetera, everything else that was addressed to the SAO and which we could not obtain otherwise. However, our wishes were one thing and will of the other members of SAO Semberija and Majevica was another. They did not express their approval that they would accept us. That is, I never saw this approval. We could have been accepted but then we did not get approval and we could have for this distribution of aid -- humanitarian aid and oil.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you ever take part in certain sessions of SAO Semberija and Majevica and upon instructions of the Municipal Crisis Staff? Were there such cases or did this document remain on paper only?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were no such cases because I was not accepted by the organs of the SAO Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Usher. Could we have P124, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I think the Prosecutor asked you about this decision on representing the Serb people of Bosanski Samac. This is on page 8 of the Official Gazette of the Municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the English version should be -- it's page 13, I believe, ERN number 00479569.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, since there were some misunderstandings there with regard to representatives, delegates, deputies, and so on and so forth, I would now like to ask you the following: Did you have a decision of the National Assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina stating that you were a full-fledged delegate to the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Usually all delegates have their delegate IDs. Did you ever have a delegate ID, an ID for parliament, an ID as member of parliament?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to me nevertheless the point of this decision, because obviously it is contradictory to what you said here, and could you explain the point of this decision. You or somebody else on behalf of the Samac municipality, did you perhaps go as observers or whatever? Could you give us some details in this regard, if you know about it.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In this decision, it says that Mirko Dragic and I are representatives of the Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under a formation. We were invited only once, as far as I know, when the Samac and Pelagicevo municipality was split into two. We were supposed to represent both municipalities. The assumption was that we would be invited when laws are to be passed, laws that have to do with the municipality of Samac. However, I never got such invitations again. That is to say, that I was not invited to represent the Municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When the Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo were split up, were you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have the right to vote?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have the right to formulate assembly conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have the right to take part in assembly committees?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Usher. I've finished with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the subject matter related to the other SAO, Northern Bosnia, that is, the Prosecutor showed you an excerpt from some minutes, and then he referred to some kind of voting or whatever. And now I'm asking you the following: In December 1991, were you in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What were you doing there then?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was doing my residency. I worked tat Doboj hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you attend this session of the SAO Northern Bosnia when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The first part of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you explain this to me.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I had a break for breakfast, and I used that time to go to that session. It so happened that the first part of the session coincided with my break for breakfast, and then after that I returned to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you ever informed by anyone that you were elected vice-president of this SAO?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it did not work, it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your answers, the ones you gave to the Prosecutor, do I understand them correctly, that you cannot even say that you were a member of a non-existent body? So were you giving answers to the Prosecutor in that context, or was there some other reason? Could you please explain this.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I explained to the Prosecutor that I was not given a decision in writing, that I did not hold this position, and that this SAO did not operate and that my municipality never opted for being a member of this SAO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you a delegate on that occasion in Doboj, at that assembly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's the way I was treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, Exhibit P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put this on the ELMO, the Serb version. Now, tell me, where is this decision? Could you find it. Right. Could we please see the top of the page too. Yes, right. Stop. Tell me, what number of the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska was this decision published in? What number is this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The number is 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's the page?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The page is 866.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The 26th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this: You personally, Dr. Blagoje Simic, did you know about this decision in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you first obtain any knowledge about this decision and about those parts of that decision?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: When I got this Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that? You don't have to remember the exact date, but...

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
