utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wish to ask you a few questions by way of clarification regarding Stevan Todorovic. You talked about him in various situations and regarding various circumstances. Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber how come Stevan Todorovic always had the opportunity of attending sessions of the Crisis Staff and the executive board and how could he hold the office of chief of police and everything else? Could you explain this a bit, if you know. What was his way of behaving so that he was in every broth, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have no objection to questions about Todorovic, but that's at least four or five different questions. Could -- could we just limit. Which question do they want to ask and even ask them separately, or -- that's at least four or five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Break them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, could you explain this in your own words, what your impression was concerning Stevan Todorovic in that period, in 1992 and in 1993. Could you explain this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The impression was that he did not discharge his duties professionally and responsibly, that is to say, the office that he was appointed to, and he did not do this the way we thought it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The very fact that he was physically present, regardless of whether he was invited or uninvited, at sessions of the Crisis Staff, does that mean that he was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe a few situations so that we could see in which way he came to the Crisis Staff sessions. Did he request something? Did he want something?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That was done in an improper way, but I would leave it to the other witnesses to testify about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us this: When his ministry, meaning the Ministry of the Interior, and his immediate superior that you spoke about, Andrija Bilosevic, who was chief of police in Doboj and other police officials, when the investigation against him was launched, can you tell us what was his attitude with respect to you personally and if you know with respect to other members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He wanted to take his revenge and he verbalised threats in a sense that nobody should dare to remove him from office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how did this end? In which way? Because we know that he was not removed, and can you tell us thanks to whom he was not removed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Thanks to his superiors. He was removed, but later on. However, he was fortunate enough in that the ministers changed almost every three months, and during that time six or seven Ministers of the Interior served, and none of them had enough time or courage to dig into this problem, and the first one that summoned enough courage removed him from office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit -- well, I don't need -- sorry. Sorry. I will just discuss that with the defendant directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we spoke about the trial before the military court -- or rather, your statement given to the military investigative judge, and I believe that was in December of 1992. Please tell me this, if you remember: Did the investigative military judge then dictate the content of your statement verbatim, truthfully, or did he dictate it the way he interpreted it or the way that he understood it? I would like to know how was that statement dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can ask him -- or I would suggest he could ask him if he dictated it verbatim or if he dictated it in a summary form, but you can't ask this man did he dictate it how the prosecutor -- the investigative judge understood it mentally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So even truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's not the form of my question regarding to the understanding of investigative judge. Furthermore, my colleague from the Prosecution put to Dr. Simic many witness statements and asking him to comment what was the personal or mental, you know, element of these statements. But I will rephrase this question. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please tell me, you mentioned then that the judge dictated that in the sense of what you were saying. Were you able then to follow in a concentrated and accurate way what the investigative military judge was dictating to the typist that was present there then?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, November and December of 1992, was there in Samac and elsewhere in Republika Srpska a conflict between the military and civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in Samac specifically. Can you tell me, please, what was the motive of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a conflict of jurisdiction. The military took in their ranks all able civilian population, then they requisitioned vehicles, trucks, and so on. They had checkpoints on the roads. And they started controlling the entire way of life, which is something that we, who had no power and were not numerous, we tried to maintain civilian authorities in wartime conditions and that was the core of that conflict. There was crime present as well. A lot of it had to do with the army. The soldiers' brigades came and went. They were stationed there and then left many problems after they left, and those problems were not solved. So we had problems daily throughout those three years. Then there were also arrests. In Samac municipality civilian officials were arrested. In other municipalities presidents of municipalities were arrested. And on one occasion, even the Minister of Defence was arrested and thrown into a pigsty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I wonder whether, Dr. Simic, you could explain your answer, "No," on line 17 of page 49 to the question posed by Mr. Pantelic, where Mr. Pantelic says, concerning the investigating judge dictating. He asked you: "Were you able then to follow in a concentrated and accurate way what he was dictating to the typist?" And you simply said, "No." I'm just wondering whether you could just very briefly say why were you not able to follow what was being said. And if you couldn't follow, why then did you sign the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was unable because in that room there were several people, and there was a conversation conducted at the same time. It was impossible to conduct a conversation and follow what was being dictated. There were two judges. One was talking to me. Then there was Stevan Todorovic there, who gave his comments on every question. Secondly, my health was very poor at the time and it was difficult for me to be concentrated on what I was saying. I was not mentioned -- I was not told at all what kind of a statement it was, and this is why I didn't hire a lawyer. I didn't have legal counsel who would be there with me and assist me in giving that statement. And what was of most importance at the time was that the attitude they had. Those were military prosecutors. They had military escort. And they came in there as though they were about to arrest me. I didn't know whether I was going to be arrested or not, because previously there were cases where presidents of municipalities were arrested. And in our municipality, we had a case where the prime minister of the municipal government was arrested. In war one never knows what's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just the last part of the question: You signed the document, even though you say you couldn't concentrate and really understand what was being dictated. Why, therefore, did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that I had an alternative. Had I not signed it, perhaps they would have arrested me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether you felt fear, and if so, what was the level of that fear at the time when you gave that statement and signed it in the presence of the military investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether I felt fear. I felt discomfort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that at the time preparations were made for this session of the municipal assembly, were there any indications or were there any steps taken by the military authorities to take over politically that assembly, or rather, the civilian government? Was it that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was that very period of time when the military in Samac municipality attempted to convene the civilian assembly and issued invitations to assemblymen of our municipality. That means that they tried to take over the control over civilian parliament in an illegal way and to convene that session. However, only one assemblyman responded to the notice to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did all of these influences contribute to your feeling of discomfort and your feeling of concern for your existence and your life?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a feeling of concern and I felt threatened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you could have been arrested by the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That wasn't unusual at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained and I think we've belaboured this matter for quite some time. Can you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, Exhibit P75.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question regarding this document: Did you dictate this letter to the professional staff or to the typists at the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you know, who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The executive council of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, regarding the local radio station, you described in detail the problems you had regarding it. I'd like to know the following: In those first few months of 1992, in April and in May, did that radio station work at all? Did it work continuously? Or did it work only occasionally?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The information that I had was that the transmitter had burned down in the beginning of the war, between the 16th and 17th of April, on the night when the elementary school burned down. That transmitter for short waves was located on the roof of the elementary school. During the first days of war, we tried to buy another transmitter; however, we found an old transmitter which was used for medium waves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you proceed, when you say: "We tried to buy another transmitter." Do you mean the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that the executive council discussed at the Crisis Staff. Executive tasks were carried out by the executive council. So that means that the executive council was the one who procured, bought the transmitter. However, they made a mistake and they bought an old transmitter that operated on medium waves and was obsolete, so that many people did not have radios in their homes for medium waves because they were outdated. So throughout the war, the radio station suffered through with this old transmitter and very few people, in fact, listened to radio broadcasts because of that, and almost nobody recorded broadcasts. I personally didn't hear a single radio broadcast. I think that it was only in 1997 when the municipality managed to buy a real transmitter, UHT, that had 1 kilowatt power.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very shortly. Let's go back to my question. May/June of 1992, did the radio station work at all? Did it not work? Or did it work occasionally?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear radio broadcasts at all during the first days of war. Later on the other transmitter for medium waves was bought, and that transmitter operated when we had electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, regarding Zasavica, were Serbs present in Zasavica as well? I'm speaking now about 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Serbs in Zasavica even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any new residents in Zasavica who were ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Refugees from other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how were they housed in Zasavica and in other villages in the territory of Samac municipality? Just say that in a few words, please. We are now speaking of Serbs who were refugees.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think there's a decree of the government of Republika Srpska regulating this, and there was also the Ministry for Refugees that regulated that through their branch office in the municipality. There was also a commission for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- no, we'll come back to that later. No, tell us this first: The municipality of Bosanski Samac, in terms of its boundaries in 1992, did it remain the same after Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the municipality of Samac in 1992 had a certain territory. What I would like to know is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think this is outside the scope of cross-examination. However; if it concerns a document that they'd like to bring in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought it was dealing with something like the decision to keep -- to make the boundaries such that Serbs are on their own and the other ethnic groups are on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a part of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I will withdraw. No problem. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to this subject. So the territory of the municipality of Samac from 1992, after Dayton, was it the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to answer yet. Could you focus, please. Just take it easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...please. 31/1. It should be a map, I think. Please, Ms. Usher, could you put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a pen - don't write anything on this map - just point out to us the territory of the municipality of Samac, Bosanski Samac from the period before conflict broke out in 1992. Try to explain this line. What was this municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: On the left bank of the Bosna River, Prud, then the border, the border along the Bosna River to Milosevac, then Gornja Slatina, Donja Slatina, Obudovac, Domaljevac, Bazik Grebnice, Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. So this thin black line is actually the territory of the municipality of Samac in 1992 before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, after Dayton -- first of all, do you have any personal knowledge regarding the Dayton boundary, and what could these red lines be, the ones that are going across the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that it is precisely this red line that shows the boundaries of the municipality of Samac and the municipality Bosanski Samac Domaljevac, or rather, the boundary towards Odzak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Pantelic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that is the Dayton boundary line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during 1992 and 1993, if you know, towards Domaljevac, where was the front line? Could you please show that.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it almost coincides with the Dayton line. It's somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, the defendant just pointed out the red line which, to his words, is the Dayton line from the town of Samac and to the south-east of Samac, above the -- above the village of Brvnik on the Exhibit D31/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me now, Dr. Simic: In 1992 and 1993 -- so to the north of this red line that I've just referred to -- out of the three ethnic groups -- or rather, the three constituent peoples, who lived on that territory?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: North of this line there were only Croats living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that mean that is that was the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Samac Domaljevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And which ethnic group lives to the west of this red line which is -- which goes more or less along the Bosna River?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to this part?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. I'm just referring to this part of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The village of Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And other villages. Who lives there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The Croats, in the village of Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now -- answer this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you can take this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now asking you the following: You personally, did you have a plan -- did you want to ethically cleanse the municipality of Bosanski Samac and did you want it to be an exclusively Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The members of the Croat people, throughout 1992 and 1993, were they in their territory, the one that they hold today as well?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have further questions for the defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Then the defendant can go back to his seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- yes. Thank you. I think that the witness unit made certain arrangements with the next Defence witness, I believe. He should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He should be -- yes. The usher can go and collect the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you escort the Defence witness. Thank you. And in the meantime, Your Honour, due to the fact that our break was a little bit changed today, what is our schedule for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will have a break at 1.00 for 10 minutes only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For 10 minutes. Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At 1.00 and then continue up to 13.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 13.45, yes. Okay. And also, if you'll allow me, Your Honour, in the meantime, what is our schedule for Monday? What would be our working hours? Do we sit in the afternoon? Or I will check that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You check the calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, we know that it's afternoon session, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if there are some changes or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not that I know of as of now. It may change over the weekend because I heard some other Trial Chambers discussing changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So just keep checking. But otherwise, it's Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. Sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness. Could you please introduce yourself. What is your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm Mirko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation? Is everything all right with your headphones? Please, if you have any problem regarding the interpretation or anything or any technical matters, please draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to this straight away so that we could address it.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also, I would like to ask you the following: Since I assume that this is the first time that you are involved in such procedure, after my question, could you pause for a few seconds so that it could be interpreted into English, so that the interpreters could also record my question and your answer and finally so that the transcript would make sense. Thank you. So Mr. Lukic, tell me, where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of January, 1958 in Gornje Slatina, municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where was your father born?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: There, not far away from the place where we live nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So also in the territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about your mother?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about your paternal grandfather? Where was he born?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Where my father was born too, in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not to go into your family tree now. Perhaps you've investigated this. But you could tell the Trial Chamber since when approximately has your family lived in this area.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say that I did investigate my family tree a bit and that my family came there sometime in the mid-eighteenth century, to this area where my forefathers lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that is basically the territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, or rather, Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, are you married?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm the father of three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you have sons, daughters?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I have three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known thing among our people that who has daughters is quite active. Tell me, where did you complete elementary and secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Gornje Slatina, in my village, and secondary school in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you continue your education after secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did continue, and I entered the University of Sarajevo in 1977 to study law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we are colleagues, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I graduated on the 6th of April -- no, the 6th of June, 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps pass the bar examination?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Last year, in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So practically now, according to law, you can be an attorney at law or a judge or a prosecutor? Is that what the regulations say in Republika Srpska, or rather, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have thus created conditions for myself to work as a judge or prosecutor or to have an office as an attorney at law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I presume, Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: -- that the recent history of Mr. Lukic qualifying in 2001 has some relevance, or not? I'm just wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, basically it's just a -- I would say a biographical profile of the witness so that we could know that if we are entering into certain interpretation of certain legal aspects of the decisions, stuff like that, that we have here in fact -- of the profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Fine, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the transcript, page 62, line 6. It's -- it was Judge Williams who asked the question and not Judge Mumba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, for the correction. I think the colleagues from the court reporting unit will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you graduated from university in 1981. Did you do your military service? Did you serve in the military in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1982 in Varazdin, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in which field were you then? In which armed services were you engaged?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I remember, yes. I was an artillery scout on 105-millimetre Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Upon completing your military service and when you started working, were you called up for military training and exercises as a reservist, or did you have a specific post? Could you explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I was not called up for military training and exercises because my war assignment was in the municipality. I worked in the municipality in a particular line of work, so all of it had to do with my wartime assignment in the municipality, with my actual line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So at that time this was in line with the existing regulations from National Defence, and these procedures probably.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The law on national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you find a job? Where was your first job after graduation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of September, 1981 I got a job at the municipality, and I was engaged in looking into the origins of property. This was an independent agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That didn't make you very popular in town, did it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that was sometime after Tito's death, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did you do specifically? What kind of a committee was it that investigated the sources, the origin of somebody's property?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: There were regulations at the time providing that at the municipal level there was special agencies which had to determine personal assets of an individual. And if it was determined that something -- some property was not properly taxed, then that individual could be requested to pay proper tax assessment on that property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that was -- that had to do with fiscal matters, with tax issues.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the assumption was that they tried to evade paying taxes, and we had to determine that and to make sure that taxes were properly paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, what was your professional post, the following professional post? What title did you have next?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: After I completed my military service, I was head of inspection at the revenue -- Internal Revenue Agency, up until 1985, and then in 1985 I became head of the Internal Revenue Agency in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, from 1985 to 1987, you had two posts, didn't you? What did you do at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1986 I was assigned to work as a temporary executive at the Stil company which was within Sipad corporation, and I was there as the bankruptcy executive. There were regulations saying that if there were conditions for reviving a company, then a bankruptcy manager would be appointed who would try to revive the company within one year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you move fast through this period and we can get to the case, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please tell me, what was your post in 1987?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I stopped being bankruptcy manager, and I resumed my post of chief of Internal Revenue Agency in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, we are in -- going to turn to other matters. And could you please tell us, what position did you have in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Up until the multi-party elections, which were held in the fall of that year, I held the post of the chief of Internal Revenue Agency, and then after the elections, I was an official without a portfolio within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. So if I understood you correctly, the elections were held in autumn of 1990, and after the new municipal government was constituted, you did not have your previous job; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was in power then in the municipality of Bosanski Samac? I mean, in terms of political parties.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: After the elections, the new political party majority was established, the coalition majority, which naturally determined the executive and the legislative power. And there were members, representatives, of the Croatian Democratic Community, Party of Democratic Action, and Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, please tell me, I assume that in this coalition agreement there were certain posts specified within the municipal government, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Like everywhere else in the world, after the election the coalition majority distributed these offices among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of one of these three political parties which established the coalition at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of some other political party?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The Union of Reformist Forces of Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time Ante Markovic was prime minister of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He was prime minister of the Federal Executive Council, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And he's a Croat by ethnicity, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this alliance of Reformist Forces was a multi-ethnic political party which advocated preserving Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the principles of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After these elections in the territory of Samac municipality, who was appointed Chief of the Internal Revenue Agency, after you were removed from office?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the assignment of posts, the SDS was given that office, and Pero Safranovic was appointed chief of that agency. He's from a village in the vicinity of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did he actually assume that post? I mean, did he start working there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The rule was that following the appointment of the new executive council, the new executive council would take over all the authorities, all the documents from the old one, and he came once or twice to see me and I wanted to turn everything over to him. It was all prepared and greed on. However, he never assumed the post of Chief of Internal Revenue Agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After these elections in 1990, what was the procedure that pertained to municipal officials? Did they remain in their posts, or were they removed from office and then some other people were appointed? Please explain to me how did this municipal procedure look like.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Some of old officials were re-elected to posts, either same or different ones, and pursuant to the law on state administration, some were officials without a portfolio. I was one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did that assume, this term, "an official without a portfolio," in terms of your salary, your duties, and so on? How long did this last for?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I could remain as an official without a portfolio for six months, receiving the salary that I had prior to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, in multi-party elections in 1990, did your party win any seats in the local parliament?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Out of 50 assemblymen, we won three seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was president of the municipal board of your party in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Director of Uniglas company, and let me just try and remember his name. Esref Ziambegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity [Realtime transcript read in error "municipality"]?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether you ever became a member of the SDS. And if so, please tell me when.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. And when were you elected? You can tell me just approximately -- vice-president of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...I mean, we have noticed a couple of things in the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, okay, the name that the witness mentioned was actually Esref Zaimbegovic. But this is not so important. But next row, it's row 25, page 67 -- it says what was his municipality? And the answer was, "He was a Muslim." It doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the -- it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It should be corrected in the transcript. So on page 67, line 25, my question was, "What was his ethnicity, or ethnic background?" Just a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's pick it up again. When were you appointed vice-president of the executive council of the Serb Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo under formation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff appointed me on the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you then head of Internal Revenue Agency as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, according to the law on state administration, there were two possibilities when it came to the election of the vice-president. One option was to have him perform his duties as a volunteer, and the other one was to have him perform his regular job, plus to have this duty as well. So I remained head of the Internal Revenue Agency, and at the same time I became vice-president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you become president of the executive council of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometime in June, around the 20th or June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what posts did you have following that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1996 I was elected president of the municipal assembly. In 1998 I was re-elected in the elections president of the municipal assembly. In 2000 in the elections I was elected head of the municipality, because in 1999 there was a new law passed on local administration and self-rule which in a different way regulated the functioning of the local government. So the post of the head of municipality was introduced, unlike in the previous times when we only had the president of the municipal assembly and the president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since it is not quite clear in the English translation, I will have to ask a few more questions. Please tell me, in our legal and constitutional system, president of the municipal assembly is also an assemblyman, a delegate to the municipal assembly, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it can't be any different because he is one of the assemblymen elected in the local elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to decision making and voting, he has one vote or more in view of the post he holds. So does he have just one vote, like everybody else, or is it regulated in a different way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the answer is given, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is my learned friend -- is Mr. Pantelic talking about now or during the indictment period in relation to the make-up of the municipal assembly? Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I will just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, we are now speaking of the time period before this post of the head of municipality was introduced. So that means the time before that, 1992, 1993, 1994. We're speaking about an entire period of time before this post of the head of municipality was introduced. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the entire time, up until 1990 time [As interpreted], there was the post of the president of the municipal assembly and the president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since you are a lawyer and you're a municipal official, please tell us, explain to us the post of the president of municipal assembly. What kind of a position is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, that person is an assemblyman representing the assembly, preparing the work at the sessions of the assembly, convening sessions, managing the sessions and signing the conclusions that were passed at municipal sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We've already said that that person has the same right of vote as other assemblymen; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the municipal assembly is -- has an equal status. He can discuss any issue just like any other assemblyman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to voting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to voting, everybody votes, and so does he. He votes, together with others. He either votes for or votes against or abstains from voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that position in itself does not give any legal possibility for him to impose any documents ex officio, through the post that he holds.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: No. The decision has to be approved by the majority in order for him to approve or dictate that conclusion, regardless of whether he likes that conclusion or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that there was a change in the law on local government and local self-rule in 1999, and can you tell us whether in Republika Srpska after that there were any elections held and how was this -- how was this law passed. Please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In April of 2000 temporary election commission of OSCE scheduled the elections and the elections were held at a local level in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, is it correct that you are talking about 1999 and then the answer also discusses April --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The main question here is that I would like to clarify the position of Mr. Lukic now in terms of this legislative, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, we're interested in the time period covered by the indictment. That's the period you should be discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But in order to clarify that issue, the next question you will see the difference between the mayor of the town and the president of the -- it's rather, I would say, specific in our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. What the witness should be discussing is what was obtaining during the time of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because we are interested to find out what the role of the Municipal Crisis Staff was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- to make this parallel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. We just want an explanation, what was going on, who had power, who was doing what during the period covered by the indictment. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tell me, in 1992 and 1993 was there a position of mayor in the municipality of Samac. According to law, did it exist?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It does exist now, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The role of mayor only in big towns. But in smaller towns there is the head of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But in essence, it's the same, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It could be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during 1991 what is your personal knowledge with regard to a certain situation in the political sense in the municipality of Samac? In 1990, the multi-party elections were held. So from mid-1991 until the end of 1991, what are your impressions? You were a citizen of that municipality after all.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say in a few sentences the first period -- that is to say, after the elections -- was one of implementing the election results and constituting the legislative power, and also the assignment of various portfolios for assembly funds, municipal funds, and then tensions started. I think I could put it in a few words now. There are big rallies throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Samac. They were organised by the HDZ and the Party for Democratic Action, meaning that they refused to have their children sent to the JNA and they wanted those who were there to return home. Many people gathered in town. Speeches were made. And then in these speeches it could be seen that they were largely political, because when analysing them, one could see that even people who did not have any children in that army made speeches to that effect, that they did not recognise the Yugoslav People's Army, and that children should be sent back home. After that, the National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in session, and when following the work of the assembly on television, every one of us could see that there were certain antagonisms in its work and that there was outvoting with regard to a number of issues and a number of decisions that were to be passed by the assembly. Namely, the HDZ and the SDA outvoted the SDS, or rather, the Serb MPs or representatives in the national parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a second. Since you are a lawyer and since you are from that area from Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there a principle of consensus involved in the previous period before 1990? And in 1990 itself, how were these political questions regulated and parliamentary life in general, through which principles?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely, because I was not a member of these parties when this agreement was being fostered between the majority coalition. But there had to be a certain consensus, because otherwise there could be no coalition and the legislative and the executive branches could not be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina were the vital interests of all the three constituent peoples respectively invariably observed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: That was a constitutional principle, a principle enshrined in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that in 1991 you had already been a municipality official for ten years and you had the opportunity of analysing this period, reviewing it, at municipal level was this principle of protecting the interests of all the three peoples, the three constituent peoples, observed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a principle that was copied from the constitution and the statute of the municipal assembly. It was observed, but what happened at the level of the national assembly and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was then transmitted to the ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that sometime in mid-October 1991 practically the Serb MPs in the republican parliament were outvoted, and in this way this vital interest was jeopardised. How was this interest --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to Mr. Pantelic leading this way. The evidence is little value if it's not coming from the witness's mouth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is -- well, a common fact, Your Honour. It's not in dispute, I believe, that in the mid-of October the Serb delegates were overvoted by Muslims and Croats. It's a fact. It's nothing more than a fact. We could make that as a fact that's now even in dispute now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The dispute is about the words "vital interest." Not about the outvoting or the parliamentary manoeuvres. It's a loaded question that Mr. Pantelic is putting to the witness. It's assuming an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic. You break down the questions and let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Your Honour. I never mentioned, Your Honour, in my question, page 74 -- between 16 and 20, I never mentioned a word "vital interest." In fact, this witness already testified that in the statute of the municipality of Samac certain principle was enacted and then I'm going to explore that issue. So I never mentioned -- my dear colleague, I never mentioned the word "vital interest." I don't know. Could you show me now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Pantelic, I can show you. It's page 75, line 2. That's where I see the words "this vital interest."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not -- clearly I said -- I said this -- in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- nation. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's get on and avoid opinions from yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Lukic, this event from October 1991 at the level of the republic assembly, how was it reflected at local level in Samac, if there were any such repercussions. Tell me what you know.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: It was the same at local level. Again, there was outvoting, and that meant blockading the work of the assembly, because what was insisted upon were certain issues that were ethnic based, and then there was a recommendation to have a plebiscite organised and held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in terms of the work of the municipal organs, how was there a blockade? How did these events start evolving?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, a certain draft decision would be prepared for the assembly. For example, regarding taxes. And certain allocations were supposed to be made, and then depending on where this money would be allocated, then there would be obstruction or blockade or something would be forced or there would be a misunderstanding or there would be an unequal quality among the assemblymen themselves. For example, the town plan should be made. There should be town planning in a certain area, and then there would be certain allocations for that. And then, on the other hand, some resources should be earmarked for another area. So it was things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for 10 minutes only and come back at 13.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Continue examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we spoke about these tensions and this blockade in the work of the municipal authorities and secretariats. Tell me, who was then president of the executive council of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac in the period of 1991, that is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: It was Mirko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was a member of which party?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who was vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Izet Izetbegovic from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that other secretariats and organs were headed by people belonging to the different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, of course you saw your colleagues at morning briefings. You had coffee together. Do you have any recollections with regard to these details these days about the contacts you had? Where did you gather? At which office? Could you portray this for us a bit.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991 in the morning when we would come, we would first have coffee and then we would discuss our work assignments, each and every one of us in his own line of work, and then there were different offices involved from the president, for the vice-president, for the executive council, the secretaries, the heads of various secretariats, et cetera. However, from 1992 onwards as things took the political course they did, people had coffee in my office. Everybody met at my office. That's where everybody could come. And then we sat there. We'd have coffee there. We'd exchange some views and experiences. And then we would all go to our respective secretariats, and everybody would do whatever his work was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any changes there? Why, for example, did colleagues not see each other in other offices? What was the reason for that? For example, why would they all assemble in your office? You were considered to be a tolerant man, a man who was a link in a way between the three ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way, but there was some kind of tension between all three. And direct communication at such levels that were unofficial, because of course it was not compulsory to have coffee in the morning together every day. So that's how they spontaneously avoided this. One by one they'd come to see me, we'd chat, and then we'd all go to our respective duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During these meetings, did anybody from the municipal administration perhaps talk about weapons or show weapons or ammunition? Do you remember anything in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I must say that even the socialising in my office lasted until, say, the beginning of April 1992. There was an incident when the vice-president of the executive council, Izet Izetbegovic, one morning was a bit nervous and he was walking around the office and we were drinking coffee and he was shaking something in his hands, and I thought it was coins, and nobody really paid any attention to this. However, the next morning again he came and again he was doing this same thing, again shaking hand with something in then. And then somebody, I can't remember what it is, said, "What is that in your hands?" And then he showed us his hands and he showed us about ten or so bullets of 5.6 millimetre calibre for a small calibre gun. I know that there was quite a bit of commotion. Then Mirko Jovanovic reacted strongly and he left the office and we never sat that way again. We didn't have coffee that way any more before, except when there were sessions of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the comment then, the one given by Izet Izetbegovic about the point of this ammunition, the origin of that ammunition? Did he make any comments to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: He was asked "Where did you get this?" He said, "Last night these past few nights whatever, we were distributing weapons and ammunition and these remained in my pocket." That was the comment, and that's why there was all this commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When he said "we," who was he referring to? What was your understanding then? Did he give an explanation? Who was "we"? Who was distributing weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He meant the Muslims, or rather, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, in relation to this atmosphere in Samac, in the period from January to April 1992, were there any armed incidents or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before I -- before Mr. Pantelic goes on, I'm objecting and I'm objecting now to the question he's just put in relation to Izet Izetbegovic's activities supposedly with a handful of bullets one morning. The -- Mr. Pantelic, I think, told us he was going to give us his proofing notes. He told the Trial Chamber, I think, last week that he was going to provide the Prosecution with something setting out the facts about which he was -- this witness was going to give evidence. There's nothing in the facts with which we have been provided as to Izet Izetbegovic having bullets in his pocket or talking about distributing weapons the night before. In that sense the Prosecution is taken by surprise as to a fact -- not the issues but as to a specific fact about which he's given evidence. So I object to him asking questions which are not -- on facts which are not outlined in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't -- obviously we don't object to him asking questions. But as long as we have some notice of the facts about which he's going to be leading evidence. This has just come from nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is well-known fact in this particular case, according to the evidence, maybe my learned friend, Mr. Re, was not familiar with that because she came later -- he came later, sorry -- that many witnesses, including Mr. Izetbegovic -- Izet Izetbegovic, actually testified about the armaments of the Muslim forces, about the TO Muslim and Croat forces, and also personal involvement in all these activities. I am speaking in light of the fact that Mr. Tihic testified that, Mr. Lukac, Mr. Izetbegovic, and many others, and we have many facts with that regard, so it is nothing by surprise here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: About the armaments of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not the point. What the Prosecution is saying that according to the summaries provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is nothing indicating that type of evidence will come from this witness. Maybe from other witnesses. But this particular witness's summary does not include that part of the evidence which you are trying to draw. This is what the Prosecution are saying. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am surprised by this objection of the Prosecution because when Prosecutor's witnesses testified, they put questions to their witnesses that were not contained in the witness statements. I can confirm that. I can look this up over the weekend. But I think that my colleague, Mr. Weiner, will confirm that questions were put to every witness that were not mentioned in witness statements. We are now referring to something that is relevant for the indictment. And when it came to Prosecution witnesses, additional, supplemental, questions were put to each of their witnesses. And when we conducted cross-examination of Prosecutor's witnesses, and when we put questions regarding things not being mentioned in the statement, the Prosecutor usually told us that these things were mentioned in Prosecutor's notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's right. When new things came, we notified them. We provided them with our proofing notes. I would -- I would write a summary based on all the new things or a summary or a statement providing all the new information that was provided. Gramsci Di Fazio, the senior Prosecutor, would provide his actual proofing notes. In addition to that, they had the police reports or the witness statements for -- in certain circumstances since 1999, so three years. Here we have just a group of statements, some are very short, some are maybe a page, some are less than a page. And we were promised proofing notes. If we go back, we had a meeting among the attorneys. We were told we were going to get good summaries and proofing notes. When we had that meeting on Thursday just before we started trial, which would have been about the 7th or the 8th, we were promised -- we were told you were going to get strong summaries -- better summaries and proofing notes. When I turned over the documents which were non-Rule 68 documents, when I called Mr. Pantelic's associate, I was told when I turned over those documents, they were going to provide me with the proofing notes or a better summary of the first witness. We were told who the first witness was then. I told them we don't have a good summary. I was told, "When you hand me those -- you know, hand me any discovery, we will hand you the proofing notes or we will hand you further discovery." When I hand those things over, I said, "Where's my discovery?" They said, "Igor Pantelic will provide it to you. I don't see any reason why he won't do it. I don't have it. Mr. Pantelic is interviewing him at the hotel. You'll get it tomorrow morning."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's get on, Mr. Weiner. I have to cut you short because these were matters which should have been dealt with by the parties. And in any case, the rules oblige parties to provide summaries on topics which the witness is going to discuss. So what the parties should do is to comply with the rules. If anything, the Defence has had enough notice -- they faced the problems themselves during the Prosecution case and the Trial Chamber kept giving instructions on this. So the Defence cannot be copying the same mistakes that the Prosecution was doing. That has nothing to do with the equality of arms. Instead, the Defence should have complied with the rules. That is what's directing the proceedings, under the instruction of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The first -- the first filings didn't comply. An order was issued. Again, there was very little compliance with the order of the Trial Chamber. So that -- you can't be pleading the mistakes of the Prosecution. That won't hold. You are supposed to comply with the rules and comply with the Trial Chamber's order, because you were given that order and you were given sufficient time. So there is no excuse for going outside the summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add, please: These facts which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you haven't complied with the order as well as the rules, that's it. You'll be confined to the summaries as given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me, what is your recollection and what do you know about the time period from January to April of 1992 in Samac, in town itself, and in the environs? Were there any incidents? Was there tension between ethnic communities? Were there any events that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I can say that from my line of work, which is internal revenue, through that I had contact with all residents of Samac municipality, and I can tell you yes, there were tensions in a sense that I had to make a plan when my inspectors went to the field to verify cafes or stores or to collect taxes from farmers, I had to make sure that I sent a Croat inspector into a Croat village, that I sent a Serb inspector into a Serb village, and I sent a Muslim inspector to Muslim residents, because there was certain resistance and there was certain obstruction and I didn't want that. I wanted a good flow of work and I was hoping that things would calm down and everything would come to its place. As far as facilities, catering facilities are concerned, it was widespread occurrence that Serb young people went to Serb cafe, Muslims went to Muslim cafes, and the Croats went to Croat cafes, and all of this was caused by an incident which took place on the day of my patron saint, St. Trifun, which is on the 14th of February, when a young Muslim man played with a hand grenade in a cafe. It exploded. He was wounded together with several other patrons of that cafe. And from that time on I don't think that people mixed in cafes. People of different ethnicities seldom went to the same restaurants or cafes. Then sometime in the second half of March, in the morning - I think it was a Saturday - I was in my parents' house in our village and then I received a phone call telling me that people could not enter the town. I asked them why, and they said it was because the SDA put up roadblocks everywhere, in the direction coming from Orasje, in the direction coming from Gradacac, and so on. I tried to go into the city. It was Saturday. It was not a working day. And I couldn't enter the city. I saw the Muslims that I knew there with their trucks and large machinery, and they told me I couldn't enter the city. In the afternoon when I returned, the roadblocks were removed and people could go in and out freely. I also went around the municipality quite a lot, and in all Muslim cities -- I'm sorry, in all Muslim villages there were roadblocks and there were checkpoints where they stopped people, asked for their IDs, and so on. I knew some of the people that manned those checkpoints, but I didn't know all of them. I have to say that I didn't have any major problems myself, except that my IDs were checked and that I would generally go through those checkpoints. But this happened to me in Prud, in Croatia in Tisina, in Hasici, in Grebnica. So in all of their places, in all entry points, they had checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the presence of some paramilitary formations in the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality in the period that we spoke of, up until April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as the paramilitary formations are concerned, I cannot confirm what individuals did involved, from which side. However, at that time there were some individuals that I didn't know. Now, as to their capacity, in which capacity they were, I don't know. They were present at those checkpoints on the roads. The rumour had it that they were regular soldiers from Croatia who manned those checkpoints together with local residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any activities at the municipal level between members of political parties that formed a coalition in the municipality? Basically, were these parties involved, these parties that were in power, were they involved in any way in those checkpoints and barricades? Did they try to do anything to overcome this problem?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The following day --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a series of leading questions. The appropriate question is who to your knowledge was involved in setting up these checkpoints, not putting words into the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Avoid leading questions. Let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, my question, Your Honour, was not who set up these barricades, no. Contrary. My question to this witness was: What are the efforts of the members of three leading parties in Samac were in order to prevent this barricade, to resolve a matter, et cetera. And my question was: Did they try to do anything to overcome this problem? That was the essence of my question. But I will put the question again. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether members of the parties that were in power in Samac did anything to reduce tensions or to overcome problems, especially those problems associated with the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The following day I heard that Sulejman Tihic, Filip Pjevac [phoen], and Dr. Blagoje Simic had a meeting and that they decided to tour the entire area of the municipality in order to overcome such problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that successful, or did the barricades remain in place?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The barricades were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the presence of some special police units from Sarajevo in Samac at that time while the inter-ethnic tensions escalated?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which times is Mr. Pantelic referring to, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have in mind the time from December 1991 till April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in December -- or rather, it was winter. I don't know if it was December or January, but it could have been December of 1991. In our municipality a special police unit had arrived from Sarajevo. If I remember well, there was some 100 policemen in it, and based on what I know, they were tasked with guarding the bridge on the Sava River between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In addition to barricades in villages, were also bunkers erected, and did you observe anything of this nature, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: In early April 1992 in those places where there were barricades and checkpoints there were bunkers as well. And in some places there were bunkers -- in some remote places there were bunkers, and I know this because I travelled. My house is some 10 kilometres from my office, so I know that in Hasici in a field there was a bunker between the railroad and the village. That's a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. I wanted to see what you knew about the ethnic composition of the population of that village, but you answered that on your own. Thank you. Now, tell me, within your line of work, did you notice any activity that would tell you whether there were private businesses closing down? What went on in municipal taxing affairs in that period of time, from January to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to say that a lot of private businesses were closing down. Mostly those owned by Croats. They had to file a request with me, and then the request was sent on to the Secretariat for Economy. They had to address me first because they had to pay their tax duties and so on. So when they came to me, I would usually ask them what was the reason for closing down their shops, and usually they would tell me that they were getting out of that line of work and that they wanted to go abroad, to Germany, Austria, Italy, to find work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that the real reason, or was there something else behind that? Did you verify this as a tax agency?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Because the latter part says, "Did you verify this as a tax agency?" So it's up to the witness whether he found out what was the real reason from --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I missed that last part. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can go on, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to say that they complied with this statement saying that they were closing their shops. However, since I knew these people, I would see them frequently later on in town, which means that they did not leave the territory of the municipality and did not move elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was your conclusion? You as a civil servant, did you perhaps launch some kind of proceedings regarding this? Why did people do that? That's what we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: The reason behind this was that they didn't want to pay taxes. They tried to evade paying taxes, and they didn't want to pay the various contributions that went into the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the presence of some armed uniformed members in February and March of 1992? I mean, the town of Samac itself.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: One could notice -- or rather, everybody in town saw that from Croatia uniformed soldiers of ZNG came on a ferry and they would sit in various cafes --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is well outside the summary provided by Mr. Pantelic. There's nothing there about Croatian -- about soldiers from Croatia coming on a ferry or soldiers from Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are speaking, Your Honour, about the atmosphere, the general atmosphere in Samac in pre-war time, which is absolutely a part of the personal knowledge of this witness and all other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it's nothing specifically -- with detail that is such and such soldier with that and that name was at that time -- just a general picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes..

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From -- to the extent of the personal knowledge of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic, you can proceed. I think some details have to be got into in order to get a clearer picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I was saying that there were even certain incidents between the members of our police from, from the area of our municipality and these persons.
