I remember at one point in time that the police found -- that is what people talked about. I didn't see it with my own eyes, but people talked about it, but it is a there true event -- that on the bridge on our side the ZNG disarmed and took off the uniform of one of our policemen, Krunic, and that after that there was commotion due to that incident. What were they doing on our side? Et cetera. And they were with the special unit that was guarding the bridge. Why did they disarm our policeman? And then Dragan Lukac, as far as I know, went to the other side to intervene so that they returned Mr. Krunic's uniform and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, in March 1992 in the region of Posavina, were there any mass killings, massacres, or were there any clashes between the members of the different ethnic groups? Do you know about any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not far away, 30 to 40 kilometres away from Samac, in Brod, in Sijekovac, the armed conflict had already broken out, and that's where bloodshed already started -- actually, war already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who attacked who there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the armed conflict is not disputed. It's not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, did you notice in the period just before April -- before the 16th and 17th of April, how did the population react, irrespective of ethnicity? Did they express some concern? Did they remain in town? Did they leave town? Tell us about the atmosphere regarding your own personal knowledge about the situation in mid-April -- or rather, before mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC
utterances.text: I wish I could say that I didn't know anything about this, but in that month of April 1992 everybody was afraid of everybody. And I think that the weekends would be the most critical for all, because what happened before that in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina showed that something like that could happen in our area too, although promises were made that nothing would happen of this sort. But near my house, for example, a column of Croats from Gornica going to Slavonski Samac would often pass. Most of them were elderly people, women and children, and they were taking agricultural machinery with them. And then after the weekend some of them would come back and others would stay with their relatives. Most of them had relatives in Croatia. And Serbs did the same thing. Those that had relatives in Serbia went that way. And then that weekend would go by, and then they would come back -- some people would stay there, rather, and others would come back. Those who were employed would take sick leave, for example, and cover that time in this way. But there was tension on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the adjournment. But if you allow me, I would like to address the Court with this particular issue. Mr. Lukic is the only witness here during this extended weekend. His fellow friends from Samac left The Hague because we want to reduce the budget for their expenses. So in terms of the fact that we shall sit in the Monday afternoon, which is a full four days, and he doesn't have any friends or relatives or contacts here, could we have permission of the Trial Chamber -- of course under very strict conditions not to discuss about any matter of the case to -- because also one of the counsels are his fellow citizen from Samac. Could we have this permission in order to socialise with Mr. Lukic to -- since we didn't enter into the, I would say, contingency issues after the 17th of April. So just in terms of -- I mean, we shall -- we shall go with your decision, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think I understand what you're asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is our witness here. And due to the fact that he's alone now here without the other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- his friends. They left to Samac. They are not in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And since he will be alone for four days, do we have permission of the Trial Chamber to contact during these few days -- of course, without any -- any possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean yourself to contact Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The other colleagues -- especially my colleague Pisarevic, he's from Samac. So we will not discuss this case. But he's alone here, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. But he's in examination-in-chief, so there's no reason why there can't be contact with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding was that when the -- maybe I'm wrong. When the witness here is starting to give his evidence, that at that moment we are prevented to contact him, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- maybe the Prosecution can help us, because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We were in the same situation with the Prosecution witnesses. They -- on several occasions they asked for this kind of permission, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't object to social contact between the lawyers and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the witness, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On the weekend, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We've actually overshot our time, because the other trial is taking place in this courtroom. So we'll adjourn until Monday at 14.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: at 1.48 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of November, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
